sentences: Should we live in the city or in the countryside?
This age-old question comes up regularly, especially since many people have rethought their way of life.
The city offers obvious advantages: work, transportation, culture, and social interactions.
Everything is close, and everything moves quickly.
But this energy comes at a cost.
Housing is expensive and often small, the air is less clean, and the noise never really stops.
The countryside, on the other hand, promises calm, space, and a more direct connection with nature.
However, it also has its challenges.
Without a car, getting around is difficult, and some services are far away.
There is no universal answer.
What works for one person may not work for another.
Perhaps what matters most is not the place itself, but the fit between that place and the life one truly wants to lead.
Let's pause for a moment to consider the strangeness of what we do every night.
For about a third of our lives, we stop eating, reproducing, and defending ourselves.
We lose consciousness, immobile and unprotected, at the mercy of the first danger.
From a survival perspective, sleep is madness.
If evolution, which ruthlessly eliminates anything unnecessary or costly, has preserved this behavior in all animals, from worms to dolphins, it must serve absolutely vital functions.
Which ones?
Science has only recently lifted the veil, and the picture it paints is astonishing.
For a long time, sleep was believed to be passive: the 'disconnected' body would simply rest, and that was that.
This image has now been swept away.
At night, the brain does not shut down; it works with an intensity sometimes greater than when we are awake, but on different tasks.
The most fascinating of these concerns memory.
During sleep, the brain replays the experiences of the day, sorts the essential from the trivial, and transfers important memories to long-term storage.
It is literally at night that we learn what we experienced during the day.
Experiments show this unambiguously: with equal effort, those who sleep after learning retain significantly better than those who stay awake.
The student who sacrifices his night before the exam deprives himself of the very tool that engraves his revisions.
Even more spectacular: the discovery, in the 2010s, of a true cleaning system for the brain.
During deep sleep, the space between nerve cells expands, and a fluid comes to flush out the waste accumulated during the day — including certain proteins associated with neurodegenerative diseases.
In sleeping, the brain essentially does its housekeeping.
Housekeeping that is impossible to do while it is running at full speed, just as you wouldn't clean a street in the middle of traffic.
These discoveries illuminate the damage caused by lack of sleep, which has long been underestimated.
Prolonged deprivation affects not only mood and concentration; it harms memory, immunity, emotion regulation, and increases the risks of many diseases.
A society that treats sleep as lost time, which is cut back to be 'productive,' is therefore making a serious miscalculation.
And yet — and this is where humility is necessary — the essential still eludes us.
No one really knows why we dream, nor what purpose these absurd stories our minds create every night serve.
Hypotheses abound, but none have unanimous support.
At the heart of the most universal experience there is, a mystery remains intact.
What science clearly establishes, on the other hand, is this: sleeping is not being absent from the world.
It is accomplishing, in the shadows, a task without which being awake itself would become impossible.

sentences: Money doesn't bring happiness," says popular wisdom — before adding, with a smile, "but it contributes to it."
This proverb, with its caveat, summarizes quite well our ambiguous relationship with money: we declare it secondary while organizing our lives around it.
So, what is the reality?
The question has shifted from the realm of moralists to that of researchers, who have been studying it for decades.
Their nuanced answers are more interesting than the proverb.
The first observation is clear: the lack of money does indeed lead to unhappiness.
Poverty is nothing romantic.
It brings constant stress, closes doors, deprives of care, security, and choices.
At the lowest income levels, every material improvement translates into a significant gain in well-being.

Getting out of precariousness, being able to pay bills without anxiety, providing the essentials for one's children: here, money very concretely buys happiness, or at least the absence of a heavy misfortune.
Claiming otherwise is a luxury of those who have never lacked.
The second observation, however, is more surprising.
Once basic needs are met and reasonable comfort is achieved, the curve flattens.
Earning more continues to bring something, but less and less.
Moving from a modest income to a comfortable income changes life; moving from a comfortable income to a very high income changes it surprisingly little.
Wealthy people are, on average, hardly happier than those who are simply comfortable.
Money follows a law of diminishing returns: the first euros are worth gold, the last ones, almost nothing.
Why this exhaustion?
Two very human mechanisms explain it.
The first is habituation: we become accustomed with astonishing speed to what we possess.
The dream car, the beautiful house, the long-desired object bring intense joy — which dulls in a few months, until it becomes the normal background, barely noticed, of our lives.
The second is comparison: our satisfaction depends less on what we have than on what we have compared to others.
And there is always someone richer, so the race has no finish line.
You catch up with your neighbor only to discover a new neighbor ahead.
So what remains once comfort is achieved?
Research converges on strangely ancient answers: the quality of human relationships, health, the feeling of being useful, the time available for what we love.
Significantly, money itself makes us happier when we use it for these purposes — buying time rather than objects, giving rather than hoarding, experiencing rather than accumulating things.
It's not the amount that matters, but the use.
The popular saying deserved better than a yes or no.
Money doesn't bring happiness, but its absence brings unhappiness; it is a wonderful means, and a poor end.
Confusing it with the goal rather than the tool means chasing a horizon that recedes as you advance.
Happiness, it seems, lies elsewhere — not further down the same road, but on a completely different path.

sentences: The city hall is launching a consultation to choose the next streets to green.
Residents can indicate the places to plant trees, create strips of land, or install larger planters.
The initiative addresses a well-identified urgency: during heat waves, the concrete streets become stifling.
Trees provide shade, retain some rainwater, and make public spaces more pleasant.
But planting in the city is never just a decorative gesture.
It requires relocating utilities, sometimes removing parking spaces, and accepting that the street will change in use.
That's where the debate begins.
Some residents are asking for more trees in front of schools and bus stops.
Others fear losing parking spaces for their cars or seeing the sidewalks cluttered.
Merchants, for their part, want to be involved in the choice of streets, as the work can disrupt their business.
The consultation won't resolve all tensions, but it can make the trade-offs more visible.
Adapting the city to the climate involves concrete choices, sometimes modest, rarely neutral.
A planted tree is also a decision about how to share the street.

sentences: The first time Tom went to the doctor in France, he didn't understand anything.
In the UK, with the NHS, you don't pay for the consultation.
You make an appointment, see the doctor, and leave without paying.
In France, the system is different.
At the end of the consultation, the doctor asks for payment: about thirty euros for a general practitioner.
Tom was very surprised.
He thought that healthcare was free in France too.
In reality, it is not free: it is reimbursed.
After the consultation, Social Security reimburses about seventy percent of the price.
A complementary insurance, the 'mutuelle', often reimburses the rest.
With the Vitale card, everything is done automatically.
Tom found this system complicated.
But he noticed one advantage.
In France, you can make an appointment quickly, often in two or three days.
You can also freely choose your doctor.
"Back home," he said, "I sometimes waited three weeks for an appointment."
Each system has its strengths and weaknesses.
The British system is simpler: nothing to pay, nothing to claim.
The French system is faster, but it requires money in advance.
Tom now has a Vitale card and a mutuelle.
"It took me a year to understand," he said.

sentences: There is a trait often noted in the French education system: the relationship with error.
Historically, assessment has been built by deducting points.
You start from twenty and go down.
Error is seen as a deficiency, something to avoid.
This relationship leaves lasting marks.

Many French adults hesitate to speak a foreign language as long as they do not master it correctly — an attitude that teachers observe less in other countries, where people are more willing to jump in with limited vocabulary.
However, research on learning indicates almost the opposite.
Making mistakes and then receiving correction leads to stronger learning than simply receiving the correct answer.
Error creates an expectation, and the correction is anchored in that expectation.
Some researchers talk about 'productive errors.'
This assumes a condition: that the error is corrected quickly and without humiliation.
An uncorrected error can settle in; a penalized error discourages trying.
This distinction is essential.
It is not about valuing error in itself, nor claiming that everything is equal.
It is about considering it as a normal and informative step.
In language learning, this is particularly clear.
Those who speak poorly make progress.
Those who wait to be ready wait indefinitely, because one never becomes ready in silence.
It took me years to accept this.
Today, when I speak a foreign language, I make many mistakes.
And I am understood, which was exactly the goal.

sentences: Insects don't have a good reputation.
They sting, they annoy, and they show up in the kitchen during the summer.
Few people worry about them when they become scarce.
However, the available data is concerning.

Several European studies, including one conducted in Germany over nearly thirty years, have measured a significant drop in the biomass of flying insects — by several tens of percent depending on the sites.
Many people have noticed the phenomenon without naming it: the windshields of cars, which were once covered in insects after a summer drive, now remain almost clean.
Why is this serious?
First, for pollination.
A significant portion of crops intended for human consumption depends, either fully or partially, on pollinators.
Without them, some crops become impossible or require manual pollination, which is practiced in some regions of the world at a considerable cost.
Next, because insects are at the base of food chains.
Insectivorous birds, whose populations are also declining, depend directly on them.
Finally, for decomposition: without insects, organic matter breaks down much more slowly.
The identified causes are multiple and cumulative: massive use of pesticides, disappearance of hedges and meadows, soil artificialization, nighttime lighting, and climate change.
Measures exist at all levels: reducing treatments, replanting hedges, leaving uncut areas, and limiting unnecessary lighting.
What makes this issue difficult is its invisibility.
No one notices the absence of an insect.
We only notice, years later, that there are none left.

sentences: Managers spend, according to estimates, between a third and half of their time in meetings.
A significant proportion of these meetings is considered useless by those who attend them.
This observation is trivial.
The reasons are less so.
The first is the lack of a clear decision to be made.
Many meetings serve to inform, which a written message would do better and faster, leaving a trace that can be consulted.
The second is the number of participants.
Beyond six or seven people, the discussion becomes difficult: the more comfortable speak, the others remain silent, and the individual speaking time becomes so low that attendance loses its meaning.
The third is the default duration.
A meeting scheduled for one hour will last one hour, regardless of the topic.
The format takes precedence over the content rather than the other way around.
What works in organizations that have tackled this issue relies on a few simple rules.
Send an agenda with the question to be resolved: if there isn't one, the meeting has no reason to take place.
Limit the number of participants and make attendance optional for those who are only remotely concerned.
Reduce the default duration to twenty-five or fifty minutes, which also allows time to move around.
Finish by stating who does what and by when.
These principles have been known for a long time and are rarely applied.
The reason may be less organizational than social.
Calling a meeting remains, in many organizations, a way to show that one exists.

sentences: In large cities, the space available per person has stopped increasing, and it is even decreasing in some areas.

Natural light comes first.
A small but bright apartment is almost always experienced as better than a larger, darker one.
The orientation and size of the windows heavily influence the feeling of confinement.
Storage comes next.
What makes a small apartment unlivable is not its size but the clutter.
Without storage space, objects take up the floor, and the usable area disappears.
The separation of uses is also important.
Being able to sleep somewhere other than where you work, even with just a simple partition or curtain, significantly changes the quality of life — a fact that has become obvious with remote work.
Noise, finally, is crucial.
Poor sound insulation almost cancels out all the other advantages.
These elements are known to architects, but they are often sacrificed in projects where the price per square meter takes precedence.
Living in a small space is therefore not necessarily a bad experience.
It mainly depends on design choices that don't cost much at the time of construction.

sentences: Vaccination is one of the most effective public health measures in history.
It has reduced, and sometimes eliminated, diseases that used to kill large numbers of people.
Its principle is old and, once explained, quite intuitive.
Our body has an immune system capable of recognizing and fighting infectious agents.
The problem is that, when faced with an unknown threat, it takes time to react — and during that time, the disease can cause damage.
But the immune system has a memory.
Once it has encountered an agent, it recognizes it and reacts much more quickly the next time.
That’s why we generally only catch certain childhood diseases once.
The vaccine takes advantage of this memory.
It presents the body with a harmless preview of the threat: a weakened agent, a fragment of it, or instructions to make a piece of it.
The immune system then trains, like in a drill, without experiencing the actual disease.
Thus, in the event of a real encounter, the defense is already ready.
There is a second effect, collective, often misunderstood: herd immunity.
When a sufficient proportion of a population is protected, the agent has a hard time spreading.
This indirectly protects those who cannot be vaccinated — infants, immunocompromised individuals.
Protection is therefore not just individual.
Like any medical act, vaccination has side effects, almost always mild, to be weighed against the risks of the disease being avoided.
This calculation of benefit and risk is precisely what health authorities assess before recommending a vaccine.
Understanding this principle does not replace this assessment.
But it makes the debate clearer.

sentences: Long-distance travel, which we have come to see as enriching, now faces a difficult objection to dismiss: it pollutes, and heavily.
Air travel, in particular, is among the most intense ways to emit the gases responsible for global warming.
A round trip to the other side of the world can, by itself, weigh as much as months of efforts elsewhere.
In light of this observation, a new sense of guilt has spread among travelers.
Is it justified, and should it make us give up traveling?
We must first acknowledge the reality of the dilemma, without avoiding it.
On one hand, travel has real value: it opens the mind, brings people closer, and fosters understanding between cultures — all that we have mentioned.
On the other hand, it has a no less real environmental cost, which weighs on an already threatened climate.
These two truths are equally valid, and it is their tension that makes the question uncomfortable.
To claim that travel has no cost, or that it is not worth any cost, would also be dishonest.
Guilt, however, is a rather unhelpful response.

It gnaws without guiding, and easily turns into its opposite: by constantly feeling guilty without changing behavior, one ends up resigning to it, or outright rejecting a demand perceived as moralizing.
Individual guilt, moreover, distracts attention from collective responsibilities, which are far more decisive.
Feeling guilty neither warms nor cools the planet; only actions matter.
A more just response would be to think in terms of moderation, not fault.
Not 'do I have the right to travel?', but 'how can I travel more reasonably?'
Traveling less often, but for longer; favoring closer destinations reached by less polluting means; making long-distance travel a thoughtful exception rather than a mechanical habit.
These choices do not eliminate the dilemma, but they mitigate it, preserving the essence of what travel brings while reducing its cost.
We must also reject a common hypocrisy: the one that places all responsibility on individuals while leaving intact the structures that make alternatives difficult.
As long as trains cost more than planes, and as long as low-pollution transport remains slow and rare, it will be unfair to blame each person for their constrained choices.
The question of travel here intersects with the broader issue of a transition that must be collective to be fair.
Should we therefore feel guilty about flying?
No, if guilt leads to nothing.
Yes, however, to question, to moderate, to choose with awareness.
Travel is neither a right without cost nor a sin to atone for, but a precious good that we must learn to use more judiciously.

sentences: Science has transformed the world and our understanding of it with unparalleled power.
It has uncovered mysteries that were once thought to be unfathomable, healed ailments that were believed to be fatal, revealed the vastness of the universe and the intimacy of matter.
In light of so many successes, it is tempting to believe that it could answer all questions, and that what it cannot establish is not worth taking seriously.
This confidence, however, deserves to be nuanced: science can do a lot, but it cannot do everything, and confusing its limits with those of knowledge would be a mistake.
What science can do, it does better than any other approach: describe and explain the world as it is.

How celestial bodies move, what bodies are made of, how species evolve, what causes diseases: to these questions, and to countless others, science provides proven answers, constantly verified and corrected.
Its strength lies precisely there: in a method that subjects every assertion to the test of facts, and grants its trust only to what withstands scrutiny.
But this very strength outlines its limits.
Science answers questions about what is; it is powerless in the face of questions about what ought to be.
It can say what an action will produce, not whether that action is good or just.
It can describe life, not say what meaning to give it.
These questions — moral, existential, aesthetic — are not scientific questions, not because they are insignificant, but because they do not fall under the observation of facts.
No experiment will tell whether a life is worth living, nor what we owe to others.
We must guard against two symmetrical errors here.
The first, which could be called scientism, consists of believing that only science provides true knowledge, and dismissing any question that escapes its method as futile.
This attitude amputates existence of essential dimensions — morality, meaning, beauty — on the grounds that they cannot be measured.
The second error, the opposite, consists of using the limits of science to discredit what it establishes, as if the fact that it does not answer everything justifies doubting what it does answer.
Recognizing that science does not say everything does not in any way allow us to deny what it demonstrates.
The right attitude lies in a double respect.
Respect for science in its domain: on questions of fact, its authority is legitimate, and preferring opinion or belief to it is unreasonable.
Respect, too, for what escapes its domain: questions of meaning and value, which it cannot settle, call for other resources — philosophy, morality, experience, wisdom.
Science is an admirable tool, but a tool, not a universal oracle.
Knowing what it can do prevents us from despising it; knowing what it cannot do allows us to ask it what it cannot provide.
Between idolatry and distrust, there is room for clear-sighted confidence.

sentences: Among the ideas of justice, equality of opportunity enjoys almost universal prestige.
Its principle is appealing: no matter the inequalities in results, as long as everyone starts with the same chances and success depends on merit, not birth.
A race is fair, the saying goes, if everyone starts from the same line; what happens next depends on each person's effort and talent.
This idea, widely shared, deserves to be examined closely, as its implementation and sufficiency raise serious questions.
The first problem is that equality of opportunity, as it is proclaimed, is rarely achieved.
Claiming that everyone starts from the same line is, in most societies, a fiction.
A child born into a wealthy and educated environment benefits, from birth, from considerable advantages: a stimulating environment, connections, financial ease, a thousand invisible aids.
A child born into poverty faces, from the outset, obstacles that the other does not know.
Talking about equality of opportunity when the starting points are so different often amounts to illusion or hypocrisy.
Truly achieving equality of opportunity would therefore require much more than is said.
We would need to compensate for the inequalities of birth, providing everyone with an education, health, and an environment that neutralizes initial disadvantages.
This is an immense, costly task, never fully accomplished.

Those who invoke equality of opportunity to justify inequalities in results often forget that they are invoking a principle that is, in reality, not respected — and that, if it were truly respected, would upend the existing order.
But even assuming equality of opportunity is perfectly realized: would it be enough to create a just society?
Nothing is less certain.
For a perfectly fair competition still produces winners and losers, and the fate of the losers remains a question of justice.
Should we abandon to their misery those who, in a fair race, came in last?
Would a society that ensured equal chances but left the defeated without dignity or resources be just?
Equality of opportunity organizes the competition; it says nothing about the treatment of those who lose it.
There is more.
The very idea of merit, on which equality of opportunity rests, is fragile.
For talents, energy, and the capacity for work, which determine success in a fair competition, are themselves largely gifts, inherited or received, for which no one is truly the author.
Does someone who wins because they are more gifted fully deserve their victory if they did not earn their gift?
Equality of opportunity shifts the lottery of birth without abolishing it entirely.
Therefore, equality of opportunity is a precious ideal, but neither fully realized nor fully sufficient.
Precious, because a society that approaches it is better than one where everything is determined by birth.
Insufficient, because even if perfect, it leaves intact the questions of the fate of the losers and the dignity owed to all.
Justice is not limited to organizing a fair competition; it also concerns what we owe to each person, winner or loser, in a society that aims to be humane.

sentences: If there is one area where the British claim uniqueness, it is certainly humor.
The term 'English humor' is one that the French themselves use, with a mix of admiration and perplexity, to describe a way of joking that partly eludes them.
This particular humor — deadpan, self-deprecation, unflappable absurdity — deserves our attention, as the way a people laughs reveals a lot about who they are.

British humor is first recognized by its taste for deadpan: saying the funniest or most absurd things without losing an unflappable seriousness, without the slightest smile, leaving it to the listener to grasp the joke.
This form confuses those who are not used to it: one does not always know whether to laugh, whether the other is joking or speaking seriously.

This is precisely where its power lies: humor arises from the gap between the seriousness of the tone and the absurdity of the content, and from the shared pleasure of perceiving it without it being highlighted.
Self-deprecation is another major trait.
Where one might seek to elevate oneself, the British prefer to make fun of themselves, downplay their successes, and turn their own flaws into a joke.
Taking oneself seriously is, in this culture, almost a faux pas; knowing how to laugh at oneself is a mark of elegance and maturity.
This self-deprecation diffuses boastfulness, but also conflict: it is difficult to quarrel with someone who first laughs at themselves.
It expresses a certain modesty, a refusal of emphasis that the British readily associate, not without malice, with their neighbors.
This humor also has a deep social function.
In a culture that values restraint and dislikes overly direct expressions of emotions, humor offers an indirect way to say what would otherwise remain unsaid.
One diffuses tension with a joke, expresses criticism through irony, and shows affection through friendly teasing.
Laughter becomes a coded language, allowing one to communicate a lot by saying little, while maintaining that modest distance that the British hold dear.
The French, whose humor certainly exists but accommodates a more direct relationship with emotions and ideas, are often taken aback by this game.
They sometimes struggle to know when someone is joking, take literally what was ironic, or are surprised that serious matters are mocked.
Conversely, the British may find the French too serious, too quick to get worked up, and insufficiently able to laugh at themselves.
Each, through the other's humor, stumbles upon a different way of inhabiting the world.
Understanding a people's humor is therefore much more than just learning to laugh at their jokes.
It is about grasping their relationship to seriousness, to emotion, to oneself, and to others.

British humor, with its calmness and self-deprecation, expresses a whole vision: that of a culture that is wary of emphasis, prefers understatement to exaggeration, and believes that one can discuss the most serious matters as long as one knows how to smile about them.

sentences: Look up at night in the heart of a big city: you will hardly see any stars.
The night sky, which humanity has gazed at since its beginnings, scattered with countless stars, has practically disappeared from our cities, drowned in artificial light.
This disappearance, so gradual that we have barely noticed it, is a sign of a phenomenon known as light pollution — and which, far from being trivial, deprives us of much more than just a spectacle.
The cause is simple: we light up more and more, and more and more brightly, at night.
Streetlights, signs, building lights, neon advertisements: our cities radiate an artificial brightness that rises into the sky and forms a halo above them that erases the stars.
Some of this light is useful, certainly; but a considerable amount is wasted, directed towards the sky rather than the ground, illuminating deserted places and burning energy for nothing.
The first loss is that of the starry sky itself.
One might consider it secondary — after all, one can live without seeing the stars.
But that would underestimate what is disappearing.
The night sky has always nourished imagination, science, poetry, and religious feeling; it has given humanity a sense of its place in a vast universe.
Depriving entire generations of this view cuts them off from a fundamental experience, that of looking up towards infinity.
A child who has never seen the Milky Way has lost something of which he doesn't even know he is deprived.
But light pollution also has very concrete effects that have long been ignored.
Night and darkness have a biological role: countless species regulate their lives, migrations, and reproduction based on them.
By lighting up the night, we disturb this nocturnal living world: disoriented birds, attracted and decimated insects, disrupted cycles.
Our own body also needs darkness to sleep well and regenerate; constant light disrupts this need.
By abolishing the night, we disturb a biological order of which we are a part.
The good news is that this pollution may be the easiest to correct of all.
Unlike others, it leaves no lasting traces: it is enough to turn off or better direct the light for the night and the stars to return immediately.
Lighting less, lighting better, lighting only where and when necessary: these simple measures would reduce waste, save energy, restore the night to life, and the sky to the stars.
Rarely has an environmental problem had such an accessible solution.
Regaining darkness is therefore not a whim of nostalgic observers.
It is about preserving a heritage — the starry sky — protecting nocturnal life, respecting our own need for night, and stopping absurd waste.
The dark night, which we have erased without thinking, deserves to be rediscovered.
For a city that has lost even the sight of the stars would, unknowingly, have lost a bit of what connects humans to the universe.

sentences: We all recognize that we have duties to others: not to harm, to help those in danger, to keep our promises.
This ordinary morality seems obvious to us, and we believe it to be coherent.
But as soon as we examine it, it begins to falter, because it is surprisingly difficult to say how far our obligation extends, and why it stops where we make it stop.
Questioning what we owe to others reveals that our moral intuitions, so assured in appearance, rest on boundaries that nothing fully justifies.
Let's consider a simple case.

If I pass by a child drowning in a pond, and I can save him without risk, at the cost of only getting my clothes dirty, everyone will judge that I should do it, and that refraining would be monstrous.
The intuition is unanimous.
But it has consequences that we do not accept.
For if I am obliged to sacrifice something minor to save a life at my feet, why should I not be obliged to save a distant life, which I could preserve at the cost of a comparable sacrifice?
Does distance change anything about the obligation?
It is hard to argue that a child dying far from me counts less than a child dying before my eyes, and yet we live as if it were the case.
This logic, if we follow it, becomes dizzying.
It seems to imply that we would be morally obliged to give almost everything we have beyond what is necessary, as long as there are, somewhere, lives we could save.

Few of us accept this conclusion; it clashes with our feeling that a life belongs to us too, that we have the right to pursue our projects, to prefer our loved ones, to not sacrifice ourselves endlessly.
But if we reject it, we must say where and why the obligation stops — and that is where our justifications become fragile.
We readily invoke proximity: we owe more to our loved ones than to strangers.
This intuition is powerful, and it undoubtedly contains a grain of truth, as particular bonds create particular obligations.
But it cannot justify everything.
That I owe more to my children does not imply that I owe nothing to the distant child; the preference for my own can explain a hierarchy of duties, not the abolition of all obligation to others.

Between the unlimited duty that would sacrifice us entirely and the indifference that would recognize duties only to those close to us, ordinary morality occupies an intermediate position that it struggles to justify.
Perhaps we must accept that morality cannot be reduced to a single coherent principle, applied without exception.

Our obligations arise from the tension between several legitimate demands: universality, which holds that every life counts equally; partiality, which recognizes particular bonds; and the right of each person to live their own life, to not be a mere instrument of the good of others.
These demands do not easily rank in order, and moral life may consist less of applying a rule than of composing, as best as we can, between duties that pull in different directions.
What remains, at the end of this examination, is not a clear answer, but a healthy unease.
We can no longer take our moral boundaries for granted, nor believe we are off the hook with others simply because we respect ordinary morality.
Recognizing that we probably owe more than we do, without believing we are obliged to unlimited sacrifice, is to honestly inhabit the tension that constitutes moral life.

This uncomfortable clarity is better than the false tranquility of those who believe they have fulfilled all their duties — because the question of what we owe to others is not one that can be closed, but one we must learn to live with.

sentences: At the end of this long journey through the highest questions, it's time to gather a few threads around the question that runs through them all: what is a successful life, a good life, a life that, when it comes to an end, one could give their assent to?

We have seen that happiness, as desirable as it may be, cannot be grasped directly, that it eludes those who pursue it; that abundance does not satisfy the need for meaning; that freedom is not the absence of limits but self-determination.
These reflections may converge towards one idea: that a successful life is not primarily a happy life, but a life that has been given shape.
What does it mean to give shape to one's life?

It means not to endure it as a succession of disconnected moments, dictated by circumstances and impulses, but to impart a direction, a meaning, a coherence to it; it is to make one's existence something like a work of art, not in the sense that it would be beautiful or remarkable, but in the sense that it would bear the mark of a project, a choice, a will.

An unshaped life is a life that is allowed to be lived, tossed about by events and desires, without direction or coherence; a life that has received shape is an oriented life, where moments are ordered according to a meaning, where one can recognize oneself as the author, and not merely the spectator, of their own existence.
This idea sheds light on why happiness alone is not enough to make a life successful.
One can imagine a life filled with pleasures, free of pain, and yet empty, without direction, without meaning, a life that one would have let unfold without ever giving it shape.
Would such a life be considered successful?
One might doubt it.
What gives a life its value may not be the amount of pleasure it contained, but the meaning it carried, the shape that was given to it, the fulfillment of what one had to do or to be.
A life can be less happy and more successful if it had meaning, direction, coherence; a life can be happier and less successful if it dissipated without shape.
Giving shape to one's life entails several things that this journey has encountered.
It requires knowing what one values, what one's values are, what one wants to do with their existence: without this awareness, one cannot give direction to their life.
It requires making choices, and therefore renouncing, because giving shape also means setting aside, limiting oneself, preferring; a life that wants everything would be formless.
It requires acting according to what one believes, aligning one's life with their convictions, in that coherence which is true fidelity to oneself.
Finally, it requires assuming one's life as one's own, being the responsible author rather than a victim of circumstances.
This conception is demanding, but also liberating.
Demanding, because it makes life a task, a responsibility: it is not enough to live; one must give shape to their life, which requires awareness, choice, effort, coherence.
Liberating, because it places the meaning of life not in circumstances beyond our control — happiness, luck, events — but in what depends on us: the shape we give to our existence.
Even in difficult circumstances, even deprived of happiness, one can give shape to their life, impart a meaning to it, lead it according to their values.
This freedom, the freedom to give shape to one's life regardless of the circumstances, cannot be taken from us.
Thus concludes this journey through the highest questions, not with a definitive answer — there is none — but with a direction.
A successful life may not be the happiest, the richest, or the longest, but one that has been given shape: a life oriented by meaning, coherent with one's values, assumed as one's own.
This task of giving shape to one's life, no one can accomplish it for us; it is our most personal responsibility and freedom.

And for those learning a language, progressing through levels to these most demanding texts, it may be an image of what all learning, all existence is: not passively receiving what comes, but patiently giving shape to what one becomes.
For living, like learning, is not about enduring, but about shaping — and a life, like a language, is only worth what we make of it.

sentences: We often envision memory as a vast repository where the memories of our past are preserved intact, which we could simply recall to find them as they were.
This image, that of memory as an archive, as a recording, is profoundly misleading.
For memory does not preserve the past like a library preserves books; it reconstructs, recomposes, and reinvents it every time we remember.
Remembering is not about finding an intact memory; it is about recreating it, from traces, in the present, under the influence of who we have become.
This truth, established by the science of memory, upends our relationship with our own past.
Let’s consider what happens when we remember.
We do not open a drawer where the memory awaited, identical to itself; we reconstitute, from fragments, a scene that we believe we are reliving.
This reconstitution is influenced by a thousand factors: our current state, our present knowledge, our desires, the narratives we have created about that event, the questions we are asked.
The memory is not recalled; it is redone, and redone differently each time, depending on the present from which we remember.
Thus, our memories subtly change over time, recomposing with each recall, drifting away from the event they are supposed to preserve.
We believe we remember the past; in reality, we remember our last memory, which is itself reconstructed, in a chain where the original is lost.
This plasticity of memory has dizzying consequences.
It means that our past, as we recall it, is partly a construction, an incessant reconstruction influenced by our present.
The most vivid memories, those we would swear are accurate, can be partially or even entirely false; one can confidently remember events that did not happen, or that occurred differently.
The subjective certainty of a memory does not guarantee its accuracy; memory is capable of creating false memories as vivid and convincing as the true ones.
Our past, which we believe we know through memory, is thus much more uncertain, much more reconstructed, than we imagine.
Should we conclude that memory deceives us, that it is a failing faculty we should be wary of?
That would be to misunderstand its nature and function.

For memory is not made to preserve the past with the accuracy of a recording; it is made to serve us in the present, to draw from the past what is useful to us, to build a continuity that allows us to live.
Its very plasticity, which makes it unfaithful to the event, is what allows it to adapt, to integrate, to give meaning.
Memory reconstructs the past not out of failure, but because its function is not faithful archiving, but the elaboration of a living and coherent experience.
It betrays accuracy in favor of meaning.
There is more.
This incessant reconstruction of the past is the very foundation of our identity.
We have seen that the self is not a fixed thing, but a story, a narrative; and this narrative is woven by memory, constantly recomposing our past to create the coherent story that constitutes us.
Memory, by reinventing our past, simultaneously constructs our identity, the narrative unity that makes the succession of our moments a life that is ours.
Whether this reconstruction is unfaithful to the event matters less than the fact that it produces a livable story, a continuity, a meaning.
We are, in a sense, the fictions that our memory composes from our past.
This truth, far from being merely unsettling, contains a part of liberation.

If our past is not a fixed given, but a perpetual reconstruction, then we are not absolutely prisoners of what was; we can, to a certain extent, reinterpret our past, change its meaning, and recompose it differently.
Not that we can falsify it at will — the facts did occur — but we can transform the narrative we create about it, the significance we give it, the place it holds in our story.
The plasticity of memory, which makes our past uncertain, is also what allows us not to be its slaves, to rework it, to sometimes heal from its wounds by rewriting them into a more livable narrative.
Memory invents our past; but this invention, while making us uncertain of what was, also makes us, in some way, masters of what that past means to us.

sentences: We venerate the truth, and rightly so: lies disgust us, sincerity seems to us a virtue, and the pursuit of truth is a noble endeavor.
However, this veneration of the truth, however legitimate it may be, encounters a difficulty that moral reflection has faced throughout time: is the truth always good to say?
Are there truths that would be better left unsaid, cases where telling the truth would do more harm than good, where the truth would conflict with other equally important values?
This question, which seems to challenge our attachment to the truth, actually requires us to clarify its meaning and limits.
We must first distinguish between telling the truth and not lying.
Not lying means not asserting what one believes to be false; telling the truth means revealing what one knows to be true.
There is a difference between these two requirements: one can refrain from lying while not telling the whole truth, by withholding certain things, by remaining silent.
The duty not to lie is stricter than the duty to say everything; one can be obliged not to assert falsehoods without being obliged to reveal all truths.

This distinction already sheds light on the question: for while it is almost always wrong to lie, it is not always mandatory to tell the whole truth, and silence, discretion, can be legitimate where lying would not be.
Let us consider cases where telling the truth seems problematic.
There is the truth that unnecessarily hurts: should one tell someone a cruel truth that would only cause them pain, without any benefit?
There is the truth that betrays a confidence, that reveals what should remain secret.
There is the truth that, when said at the wrong time, would do more harm than good, like terrible news announced without tact.
In these cases, telling the truth conflicts with other values: kindness, discretion, care for others.
And it is not obvious that the truth should always prevail, that the duty to tell the truth always takes precedence over the concern not to harm.
Should we conclude that one can sacrifice the truth in the name of other values, that it is permissible to lie to spare, to cushion, to do good?
That would be rushing to a conclusion and opening a dangerous door.
For lying, even with good intentions, has a cost: it betrays trust, it treats the other as incapable of bearing the truth, it arrogates the right to decide what others should know.
Lying 'for the good' of others is often a form of disguised contempt masquerading as benevolence, a way of treating the other as a minor who needs to be protected from the truth.
And it opens a slippery slope, where one easily convinces oneself that lying serves the good while it serves our comfort.
Distrust of lying, even well-intentioned, remains warranted.
The correct position perhaps lies in this distinction: between lying, which must be almost absolutely rejected, and silence or discretion, which can be legitimate.
One can, without lying, choose not to say a truth that would unnecessarily hurt, to keep secret what should remain so, to consider the timing and manner of conveying a difficult truth.
It is not betraying the truth to withhold it out of respect; it is betraying the truth to assert falsehood.

Wisdom regarding the truth is not about saying everything without regard for the consequences, nor about lying in the name of good, but about never asserting falsehood while knowing when to remain silent, to be considerate, to choose the timing and manner.

There is an art to telling the truth, which is neither the brutality of those who state it without regard, nor the cowardice of those who distort it, but the discernment of those who know how to express it accurately.
This reflection brings us back to what we said about the ethics of language.
Using the truth well is not just about not lying; it is also about knowing how to convey the truth accurately, at the right time, in the right way, with concern for others.
The truth is a precious good, but it is not the only one, and the art of living often consists of reconciling goods that may come into tension: truth and kindness, sincerity and care for others.
The truth is not always good to say brutally, without regard, at the wrong time; but it is almost always wrong to betray it through lies.

Between the duty not to lie, which is almost absolute, and the duty to say everything, which has exceptions, there is room for a wisdom that honors the truth without making it a weapon, that serves it without brandishing it, that never betrays it but knows when to remain silent.

sentences: Yesterday, I had a very long day.
I will remember it for a long time!
It all started at five thirty in the morning.
I had an important meeting at eight o'clock.
So I got up very early.
Outside, it was still dark.
I quickly had a coffee, then I left.
On the train, I reviewed my documents.
At the office, there were already people.
My colleague Samir said to me: 'Are you ready?'
'I think so,' I replied.
The meeting started well.
I presented my project.
The clients asked a lot of questions.
But suddenly, I looked for an important document.
It wasn't there!
I had forgotten it at home.
I got very hot.
So I explained the problem in simple words, without the paper.
In the end, it worked.
At noon, I was exhausted.
I ate a sandwich in front of my computer, because I still had a lot of work.
The afternoon went by very quickly.
I replied to forty messages.
At six o'clock, my boss came to see me.
He smiled.
The clients accepted your project.
Well done.
I got home at seven-thirty.
I was tired, but very happy.
That evening, I went to bed at nine o'clock.

sentences: We most often use the word 'ideology' to refer to the beliefs of others, those we consider false, biased, dictated by interests or prejudices: the opponent is 'ideological', while we would be clear-sighted and objective.
This polemical usage masks what ideology really is, which is much deeper and more troubling.

For ideology is not primarily what others think; it is what makes us think what we think, without our awareness, the set of representations that seem obvious to us and which, precisely because they seem obvious, escape our scrutiny.
Ideology is less a content than an environment, the very air we breathe without seeing it.
Let us understand this deeper conception of ideology.
Every society, every era, is permeated by representations that seem self-evident, shared certainties about what is normal, natural, desirable, about how things are and should be.
We do not perceive these certainties as opinions, as positions among other possible ones; we take them for reality itself, for common sense, for what goes without saying.

Yet it is precisely these that constitute ideology: not explicit convictions that one would defend, but implicit presuppositions that structure our thinking without us questioning them, because they seem too obvious to be presuppositions.
Ideology is what thinks in us before we think, the invisible framework that guides our representations.
This concept has a formidable consequence: we are all, always, caught in an ideology, even when we believe ourselves to be the most clear-sighted.
For ideology is not something we can escape simply by goodwill, by deciding to be objective; it is the very medium of our thought, which makes it possible by orienting it.

To believe that we are outside of any ideology, that we see things as they are while others are blinded by theirs, is the very mark of the deepest ideological blindness: for it is to take the obviousness of one's own ideology for reality itself.
The height of ideology is to believe oneself to be without ideology; the one who thinks they are perfectly clear-sighted is the one who does not see the framework that structures their clarity.
Should we conclude that we are irredeemably prisoners of ideology, incapable of any truth, condemned to see the world only through frameworks that blind us?
This skeptical conclusion would be excessive and paralyzing.
For if we can never place ourselves outside of any ideology, at an absolute and neutral viewpoint, we can become aware of our presuppositions, question them, relativize them, and change them.
We cannot see without a framework, but we can examine our frameworks, compare them to others, and discover their contingency.

This clarity is never total or definitive — we always remain caught in some ideology — but it is real and gradual: one can be more or less aware of their presuppositions, more or less capable of questioning them.
The freedom regarding ideology is not to free oneself absolutely from it, which is impossible, but to make it visible, to submit it to examination, and not to take it for reality itself.
How can we gain this relative clarity?
Several paths lead to it.
Confrontation with other cultures, other eras, and other ways of thinking reveals the contingency of our own certainties by showing that we can think differently.
History, which shows that what we consider natural has an origin, has been different, could be different, deconstructs our assumptions.
Encountering those who think differently, if we truly listen to them, allows us to see our own frameworks by colliding them with theirs.
All these paths have one thing in common: they displace us, pull us away from the obviousness of our point of view, and make us see from the outside what we lived from the inside as self-evident.
To detach ourselves a bit from our ideology is to learn to see ourselves through the eyes of another.
Recognizing that ideology is the air we breathe, and not just what others breathe, is therefore the beginning of possible clarity.
This frees us from the most dangerous illusion, that of believing we are outside of any ideology, and invites us to be vigilant regarding our own certainties.

This also makes us fairer towards those who think differently: for if we are all caught in some ideology, then the opponent is not the only 'ideologue' while we would be clear-sighted; we all are, and this shared condition should temper our confidence.

In a world where everyone denounces the ideology of others while believing themselves to be clear-sighted, true clarity begins with the recognition of one's own ideology—not to renounce it, which is impossible, but to stop confusing it with the truth.

sentences: For years, I ate by the clock, not according to my real hunger.
When noon struck, I ate, whether I was hungry or not.
This habit, formed since childhood at school, had disconnected me from a natural signal: that of my own hunger.
I began to question this topic after a conversation with a nutritionist, who explained to me that many people had lost this simple ability to listen to their bodies.

She suggested an exercise that seemed almost strange to me at first: before each meal, to stop for a minute and honestly ask myself if I was really hungry, or if I was eating out of habit, boredom, or simply because it was time.
In the first few weeks, I was surprised to discover that I often ate without real hunger, driven by the time, the smell of a dish, or simply the desire to take a break in my day.
Gradually, I learned to better distinguish these different sensations, and to eat more according to my real needs rather than old habits.

This new attention to my own sensations extended, almost without my deciding it, to other areas of my life: I now perceive better the difference between true fatigue and mere lack of stimulation, or between a need for a break and a fleeting desire to procrastinate.
This change is nothing like a traditional diet.
It's not about eating less, but about eating more consciously, by relearning a signal that years of habits had ended up blurring.
This approach requires patience, but it has reconciled me with a simpler and ultimately more peaceful relationship with food.

sentences: Every summer, my city, usually quiet, completely transforms.
The streets, generally calm, fill up with visitors who come to admire our old historic center.
The café terraces, half-empty in winter, overflow with tourists taking photos.
This influx brings obvious economic benefits.
Many shopkeepers make most of their annual revenue during these few summer months.
But this same influx also changes our daily lives, not always for the better.
Lines are getting longer everywhere, even at the local bakery.
The price of rents is also rising, driven by the increase in short-term rentals aimed at tourists.
I've noticed that some residents, tired of this summer hustle, prefer to go on vacation elsewhere during this time, paradoxically fleeing their own city.
Others, like my neighbor who runs a small restaurant, on the contrary, look forward to this season, knowing it represents an essential part of their income.

Some residents have found their own ways to cope with this period: shifting their shopping hours, avoiding certain streets at the busiest times, adopting, for the summer, a slightly different pace, as if the city itself became a place they had to learn to inhabit again.
This situation gives me mixed feelings.
I understand the economic importance of this tourism for my city.
But I also feel a slight relief every year when September arrives and my city gradually regains its usual calm.

sentences: A year ago, a bulk store opened in my neighborhood, without plastic packaging.

The seller, clearly used to this kind of situation, patiently explained to me how the scales work, how to weigh my empty containers before filling them.
After a few visits, I ended up organizing a small bag of reusable jars, always ready in my trunk for my weekly shopping.
This change in habit had several unexpected effects.
First, I now buy more precise quantities, which reduces food waste.
Then, my bin for plastic packaging has significantly decreased.
Waste, too, has clearly reduced: I now buy precise quantities, suited to my actual needs, rather than standardized packaging that is often too large.
This discreet but constant change has ultimately altered my relationship with what I keep at home.
I continue to do some of my shopping in regular stores for certain products that are not available in bulk.
But this new habit, adopted gradually, has changed the way I think about each food purchase, which is now more thoughtful than before.

sentences: The idea of using video games as a true educational tool is increasingly appealing to teachers and education researchers, convinced that this medium has a largely underutilized learning potential in traditional educational systems.

This belief is based on characteristics specific to well-designed video games: immediate feedback on mistakes made, a gradual progression suited to the player's level, and above all, an intrinsic motivation that is often much higher than that observed in a traditional school setting, where learning is frequently seen as a constraint rather than a chosen pleasure.

Several studies have indeed demonstrated promising results in specific areas: some strategy games may improve the ability to solve complex problems, while games specifically designed for language learning show comparable, if not superior, results to certain more traditional teaching methods.
However, these encouraging results deserve to be qualified by several important limitations.

The design of a truly educational game, combining pedagogical rigor and authentic playful enjoyment, remains a complex task: many games marketed as 'educational' actually fail to combine these two requirements, producing either pedagogically solid but boring content, or successful entertainment that is pedagogically superficial.

The real issue is probably not to ask whether video games can educate in general, a question too broad to receive a simple answer, but rather to precisely identify under what specific conditions, for which content, and according to what rigorous pedagogical design, this medium can effectively fulfill this educational promise that is still largely experimental to this day.

One morning as she was returning like this, she suddenly thought she could distinguish the long barrel of a rifle that seemed to be aimed at her.
It was protruding obliquely from a small barrel, half buried in the grass, at the edge of a ditch.

He had gaiters buckled up to his knees, his cap pulled down to his eyes, trembling lips, and a red nose.
It was Captain Binet, lying in wait for wild ducks.

How, he replied, can you trust one another if you once break the only bond of society and trust, which is good faith?

After you have established as a principle that one can violate the rules of honesty and loyalty for a great interest, which of you will be able to trust another, when that other can find a great advantage in breaking his word and deceiving him?
Where will you be?
Which of you will not want to outsmart his neighbor with his own tricks?

What will your mutual distrust, your division, your eagerness to destroy one another be!

sentences: I pulled Benedetto aside and made him the proposal to follow me, surrounding this proposal with all the promises that could entice a twelve-year-old.
He let me finish, and when I was done, he burst out laughing:

--Are you crazy, my uncle? he said (he called me that when he was in a good mood); me change the life I lead for the one you lead, my good and excellent laziness for the horrible work you have imposed on yourself! spend the night in the cold, the day in the heat; hide constantly; when you show yourself, get shot at, and all this to earn a little money!
Money, I have as much as I want! Mother Assunta gives me some whenever I ask her.
So you see that I would be a fool if I accepted what you are proposing to me.
I was astonished by this audacity and this reasoning.
Benedetto went back to playing with his friends, and I saw him from a distance pointing me out to them as an idiot.
--Charming child! murmured Monte-Cristo.
Oh! If he had been mine, Bertuccio replied, if he had been my son, or at least my nephew, I would have certainly brought him back to the right path, for conscience gives strength.
But the thought of hitting a child whose father I had killed made any correction impossible for me.

I gave good advice to my sister, who, in our discussions, constantly defended the poor little one, and when she admitted to me that several times she had been short of considerable sums, I pointed out a place where she could hide our little treasure.
As for me, my mind was made up.
Benedetto could read, write, and count perfectly well, for when he happened to want to work, he learned in one day what others learned in a week.

My mind was made up, I said; I had to hire him as a secretary on some long-haul ship, and, without warning him at all, have him taken one fine morning and transported on board; in this way, and by recommending him to the captain, his entire future would depend on him.
With this plan settled, I left for France.

sentences: Obviously, replied the harpooner, and yet, since I've been on this floating island for three hours, it hasn't shown any signs of life.
This boat hasn't moved?
No, Mr. Aronnax.
It just sways with the waves, but it doesn't move.
We know, without a doubt, however, that it is capable of great speed.
Now, since a machine is needed to produce this speed and a mechanic to operate this machine, I conclude... that we are saved.
Hum! said Ned Land in a reserved tone.
At that moment, and as if to support my argument, a bubbling sound came from the back of this strange device, whose propeller was obviously a screw, and it started to move.
We barely had time to grab onto its upper part, which was sticking out about eighty centimeters.
Fortunately, its speed was not excessive.
As long as it navigates horizontally, murmured Ned Land, I have nothing to say.
But if it takes a notion to dive, I wouldn't give two dollars for my skin!
Even less could the Canadian have said.
It was therefore urgent to communicate with the beings trapped inside this machine.
I searched its surface for an opening, a hatch, "a manhole," to use the technical term; but the lines of bolts, tightly fastened over the seams of the plates, were clear and uniform.
Moreover, the moon then disappeared, leaving us in deep darkness.
We had to wait for daybreak to consider how to get inside this submarine.
Thus, our salvation depended solely on the whims of the mysterious helmsmen who were operating this device, and if they dove, we were lost!
Except for this case, I had no doubt about the possibility of establishing contact with them.
And indeed, if they didn't produce their own air, they must necessarily come back to the surface of the Ocean from time to time to replenish their supply of breathable molecules.
Therefore, there was a need for an opening that connected the inside of the boat with the atmosphere.

"Baron," he said, "here I am.
For a long time, we've been dancing around our old words...."

Morcerf expected, upon saying these words, to see the banker's face brighten, which he attributed to the latter's silence; but, on the contrary, that face became, almost unbelievably, even more impassive and colder.
That’s why Morcerf had stopped in the middle of his sentence.
"What words, Count?" asked the banker, as if he were vainly searching his mind for an explanation of what the general meant.
--Oh! said the count, you are a stickler for formality, my dear sir, and you remind me that the ceremony must be conducted according to all the rites.
Very well! Indeed.
Forgive me, as I have only one son, and this is the first time I am thinking of marrying him, I am still learning: well, I will proceed."
And Morcerf, with a forced smile, got up, made a deep bow to Danglars, and said to him:
"Monsieur le baron, I have the honor of asking for the hand of Miss Eugénie Danglars, your daughter, for my son, Viscount Albert de Morcerf."
But Danglars, instead of welcoming these words with the favor that Morcerf might have hoped for, frowned, and without inviting the count, who remained standing, to sit down:
Sir, the Count, he said, before I answer you, I need to think.
--To think! Morcerf replied, increasingly astonished, haven't you had time to think since we first discussed this marriage eight years ago?
--Sir, the Count, Danglars said, every day there are things that make us rethink what we thought was settled.
--How so? Morcerf asked; I no longer understand you, Baron!
--What I mean, sir, is that for the past fifteen days new circumstances....
--Allow me, Morcerf said; is this or is it not a comedy we are playing?
--How so, a comedy?
--Yes, let's clarify this categorically.

sentences: Such was the succession of phenomena that formed Iceland; all of them came from the action of internal fires, and to suppose that the internal mass did not remain in a permanent state of incandescent liquidity was madness.
Madness, especially, to claim one could reach the center of the globe!
I thus reassured myself about the outcome of our venture while climbing towards Sneffels.
The path was becoming increasingly difficult; the ground was rising; the rock fragments were shifting, and one had to pay the utmost attention to avoid dangerous falls.

Hans advanced calmly as if on level ground; sometimes he disappeared behind the large boulders, and we lost sight of him momentarily; then a sharp whistle, escaping from his lips, indicated the direction to follow.
He often also stopped, picked up some rock debris, arranged them in a recognizable way, and thus created landmarks intended to indicate the route back.
A precaution good in itself, but which future events rendered unnecessary.
Three exhausting hours of walking had brought us only to the base of the mountain.
There, Hans signaled to stop, and a simple lunch was shared among all.
My uncle was eating double portions to go faster.
However, this break for refreshment was also a break for rest, so he had to wait for the guide's good pleasure, who signaled the departure an hour later.
The three Icelanders, as taciturn as their companion the hunter, did not say a single word and ate modestly.

We were now starting to climb the slopes of Sneffels; its snowy summit, due to a common optical illusion in the mountains, appeared to be quite close to me, yet it would take many long hours to reach it! What fatigue, especially!
The stones, which were not bound together by any soil or grass, crumbled under our feet and were lost in the plain with the speed of an avalanche.

In certain places, the slopes of the mountain formed an angle of at least thirty-six degrees with the horizon; it was impossible to climb them, and these rocky inclines had to be navigated with difficulty.
We then provided each other with mutual assistance using our sticks.
I must say that my uncle stayed as close to me as possible; he never lost sight of me, and on many occasions, his arm provided me with solid support.
For his part, he undoubtedly had an innate sense of balance, as he did not falter.
The Icelanders, although burdened, climbed with the agility of mountaineers.

sentences: Common madness, when it is not incurable, can only be cured by moral means.
Medicine and therapy are powerless in this regard, and their ineffectiveness has long been recognized by specialists.
Were these moral means applicable to Thomas Roch's case? It was reasonable to doubt it, even in the calm and healthy environment of Healthful-House.
Indeed, anxiety, mood swings, irritability, peculiarities of character, sadness, apathy, and aversion to serious activities or pleasures—these various symptoms were clearly evident.
No doctor could have been mistaken about this; no treatment seemed capable of curing or alleviating them.
It has been rightly said that madness is an excess of subjectivity, meaning a state where the soul gives too much weight to its inner labor and not enough to external impressions.
In Thomas Roch's case, this indifference was nearly absolute.
He lived only within himself, prey to a fixed idea whose obsession had brought him to where he was.
Would there be a circumstance, a backlash that would 'externalize' him, to use a rather precise term? It was unlikely, but not impossible.

sentences: Ah, that's right, said Abbé Faria.
We are prisoners; there are moments when I forget it, and when, because my eyes pierce the walls that confine me, I believe I am free.
But why are you imprisoned?

Me? Because I dreamed in 1807 of the project that Napoleon wanted to realize in 1811; because, like Machiavelli, amidst all those little principalities that made Italy a nest of small, tyrannical, and weak kingdoms, I wanted a great and single empire, compact and strong: because I thought I had found my Cesare Borgia in a foolish crowned man who pretended to understand me in order to betray me better.
It was the project of Alexander VI and Clement VII; it will always fail, since they undertook it uselessly and Napoleon could not complete it; indeed, Italy is cursed!
And the old man lowered his head.

Dantès did not understand how a man could risk his life for such interests; it is true that while he knew Napoleon because he had seen and spoken to him, he was completely unaware, on the other hand, of who Clement VII and Alexander VI were.
"Aren't you, said Dantès, starting to share the opinion of his jailer, which was the general opinion at the Château d'If, the priest who is believed to be... ill?
--What you mean is that people think I'm crazy, isn't it?
--I didn't dare, said Dantès, smiling.

--Yes, yes, continued Faria with a bitter laugh; yes, it's me who is considered insane; it's me who has entertained the guests of this prison for so long, and who would delight little children, if there were any children in this place of hopeless suffering."
Dantès remained still and silent for a moment.
So, you are giving up on fleeing? he said to him.
--I see fleeing as impossible; it is a rebellion against God to attempt what God does not want to happen.
--Why discourage yourself? It would be too much to ask of Providence to expect to succeed on the first try.
Can't you start over in a different way from what you did this time?
--But do you know what I have done, to speak so casually about starting over?
Do you know that it took me four years to make the tools I have?
Do you know that for the past two years I have been scraping and digging in soil as hard as granite?

Do you know that I had to unearth stones that I would not have believed I could move before, that entire days have passed in this titanic labor, and that sometimes, in the evening, I was happy when I had removed a square inch of that old cement, which had become as hard as the stone itself?

Do you know, do you know that to accommodate all this earth and all these stones that I was burying, I had to pierce the vault of a staircase, in the drum of which all these debris have been buried in turn, so that today the drum is full, and I no longer know where to put a handful of dust?

Do you know, finally, that I believed I was close to the goal of all my work, that I felt I had just the strength to accomplish this task, and that now God not only pushes this goal back but moves it I don't know where?
Ah! I tell you, I repeat it to you, I will do nothing more from now on to try to regain my freedom, since it is God's will that it be lost forever.

sentences: Okay, just one more episode and then I'm going to bed.
Who has never said this phrase, only to betray it immediately?
It's one o'clock in the morning, the screen asks, 'Watch the next episode?', and our finger clicks almost by itself.
Series have become the main pastime for millions of people.
This success deserves our attention.
First of all, a series offers what cinema cannot: time.
A film has to tell everything in two hours.
A series, on the other hand, has ten, twenty, sometimes a hundred hours.
The characters can evolve slowly, change, and surprise us.
We see them age, love, fail, and start over.
After a few seasons, they are no longer just characters: they are acquaintances.
Some viewers cry at the end of a series like we cry at a departure.
It's not ridiculous; it's a sign that a long story creates deep connections.
Next, we must acknowledge the skill of the creators.
The end of each episode is designed to leave us in suspense: a revelation, a danger, a door that opens.
This old trick of the serial already existed in the novels of the nineteenth century, published chapter by chapter in newspapers.
The difference is that in the past, you had to wait a week.
Today, the next part is just three seconds away.
Our patience doesn't stand a chance anymore.
Series have also become a common language.
At the office, at a dinner, they replace the weather in conversations.
Talking about it means belonging to a community; comparing theories about what happens next has become a collective game.
Should we be worried about all of this?
A little, perhaps.
Entire evenings consumed by a screen, shortened sleep, books left closed: the series is a pleasure that easily takes up all the space.
I myself devoured a whole season in a rainy weekend, and I remember the strange feeling of Sunday night — that mix of satisfaction and lost time.
The solution is certainly not to stop watching series, which are among the great creations of our time.
It is more modest: to decide beforehand how many episodes we will watch.
And sometimes, to have the heroic courage to turn it off in the middle of the suspense.
The main character will survive until tomorrow.
Us too.

sentences: For years, I was the person who always says yes.
Did a colleague need help finishing a report?
Yes.
Was a friend moving on Saturday?
Yes.
One more meeting, one more favor, one more evening while I dreamed of my couch?
Yes, yes, yes.
I was proud of this reputation: people could count on me.
Always.
The problem is that this medal had a downside that I refused to see.
I was exhausted.
My weekends belonged to others.
My own projects — sports, reading, that photography course I had been talking about for three years — were always postponed due to lack of time.
And above all, an unpleasant feeling was growing inside me: a kind of quiet anger towards those I was helping.
They hadn't done anything to me; they asked, I said yes.
The anger should have been directed at the only real culprit: me.
The trigger came one Sunday evening.
I had spent the whole weekend helping three different people, and I realized that I hadn't had an hour for myself.
Not one.
Sitting in my kitchen, I understood a very simple phrase that changed everything: every yes said to others is a no said to oneself.
My schedule was full of yeses; my life was full of nos.
Learning to say no has been more difficult than expected.
The first no cost me a night of reflection — over a simple evening that I didn't want to spend.
I was afraid of disappointing, of coming across as selfish, of losing friends.
I discovered three things that helped me a lot.
First, you can say no without justifying yourself for ten minutes.
"Thank you for thinking of me, but I can't" is a complete sentence.
The more you explain, the more you apologize, the more it seems like you're seeking permission.
Then, you can suggest something else when you really want to: "I can't help you on Saturday, but I'm free on Wednesday evening."
The no becomes a choice, not a rejection.
In the end — and this was the real surprise — people accept it very well.
No one got angry.
No one stopped calling me.
My friendships have even improved in quality: when I say yes now, it's a true yes, joyful, whole, without hidden anger.
I still say yes often.
Helping others remains a pleasure.
But it has become a decision, not just a reflex.
And my Saturdays, sometimes, are finally mine.
