sentences: Statues, these objects we once thought were inert, have become the stage for intense confrontations.
Should we topple the monuments erected in honor of figures whose past offends us — slave traders, colonizers, men from another era honored for reasons we reject today?
Or should we preserve them, in the name of history, heritage, and the refusal to erase the past?
This question, which stirs so many societies, is not as simple as the opposing camps would like it to be, and it deserves more than slogans.
Those who demand the removal of statues put forward serious arguments.
A statue is not a neutral document; it is a tribute, an honor given in public space.
Erecting a statue means proposing a model, telling everyone: here is someone worthy of admiration.
But how can we justify continuing to honor, in public squares, figures who have committed or supported what we consider crimes?
For the descendants of those who were enslaved or colonized, these statues are not abstract history; they are a daily wound, the ongoing celebration of their oppressors.
Maintaining them is perpetuating a tribute that has become insulting.
Those who oppose the removal of statues also have their arguments.
Erasing the traces of a troubling past, they say, is to condemn ourselves to forget it, and forgetting has never solved anything.
Judging the people of the past by today's values is anachronistic: they were of their time, and almost all our ancestors, by that measure, would be condemnable.
Where would we stop if we set out to purge public space of everything that offends today's sensibilities?
Isn't there, in this desire to erase, something akin to a rewriting of the past, a refusal to look at it as it was, with its glories and its crimes intertwined?
Both of these positions have their share of truth, which is why the question is difficult.
But perhaps the opposition between preserving and destroying is poorly framed, as if these two terms exhausted the possibilities.
For there are intermediate paths, more fruitful than simple maintenance or erasure.
One can move a statue from a place of honor to a museum, where it will no longer be celebrated but explained, placed back in its context, offered for reflection rather than admiration.
One can maintain it while contextualizing it, adding elements that remind us of the darker side of the figure, transforming the monument into an opportunity to learn.
One can make it an object of critical memory, rather than a tribute or an empty gesture.
What really matters, in the end, is to distinguish what the statue does in public space.
As long as it stands in glory, it honors; it is this honor that poses a problem, not the existence of the object.
The question is therefore not so much 'should we destroy or preserve?' as 'should we continue to honor?'
— and to that, the answer can be no without needing to erase.
Removing an honor is not erasing a history; it is stopping the celebration of what should no longer be celebrated, while still keeping the means to understand it.
The debate about statues, beyond the objects it concerns, touches on our relationship with the past.

It reveals that this relationship is never fixed, that it is re-discussed with each generation, and that the public space, where the past is visible, is also a place where the present asserts its values.

Neither the conservatism that wants to keep everything intact, nor the iconoclasm that wants to erase everything does justice to the complexity of the task: to assume a past in its truth, without continuing to honor what no longer deserves it.
A mature society is neither one that blindly venerates its monuments, nor one that tears them down in a frenzy, but one that knows how to both remember and judge in their presence.

sentences: Well, we'll thaw him out.
Thomas Black, carried by the sergeant, the corporal, and the courier, entered the fort's house.
He was placed in a first-floor room, where the temperature was quite bearable, thanks to the presence of a stove glowing red hot.
He was laid on a bed, and the captain took his hand.
That hand was literally frozen.

They removed the blankets and fur coats covering Thomas Black, tied up like a package, and under this covering, they discovered a man about fifty years old, large, short, with graying hair, an unkempt beard, closed eyes, and lips pressed together as if they had been glued shut.
This man was no longer breathing, or barely so, that his breath would hardly have fogged a mirror.
Joliffe was undressing him, turning him over and over quickly, while saying:
"Come on! Come on! Sir!
Aren't you going to come back to yourself?"
This person, arriving under these circumstances, seemed to be nothing more than a corpse.
To bring back the lost warmth in him, Corporal Joliffe saw only one heroic means, and that means was to plunge the patient into hot punch.
